# Payments API reliability capacity notebook

Synthetic authored notebook, recorded 2026-10-08T08:00:00Z.

## Connection acquisition definition

Connection acquisition is the interval between requesting an application connection and receiving a usable lease. It includes waiting for a free slot but excludes SQL execution after checkout. In the Payments API reliability rehearsal, the caller's end-to-end latency therefore cannot identify a slow query by itself. The retained phase split records acquisition p95 at 1850 milliseconds while command execution stayed near its earlier range. A diagnosis must compare these spans on the same request cohort rather than subtracting unrelated percentiles.

The acquisition clock should begin at the application pool boundary rather than at gateway ingress. If the client library creates a physical connection while fulfilling the lease, that creation time belongs to acquisition but should have its own child span for interpretation. Authentication, name resolution and transport setup can then be compared without relabeling all acquisition delay as a queue. A successful lease also differs from an acquisition attempt that exhausts its deadline. Reviewing only successful leases discards the worst waits, so the notebook keeps attempt outcomes alongside durations. These are proposed instrumentation distinctions, not claims that additional spans were collected in the original rehearsal. A reader should be able to explain which interval the observed percentile describes and which missing observations still prevent attribution.

Percentiles are summaries of distributions, not additive pieces of one representative request. Adding acquisition p95 to execution p95 may combine two different requests and overstate a tail; subtracting them can manufacture a residual that no request experienced. For a phase explanation, use paired spans on the same retained request when available and describe marginal distributions separately when they are not. Report sample count and failed-attempt count with each percentile. A narrow healthy sample can support a narrow statement, while an absent pairing cannot support a precise decomposition of end-to-end time. This distinction matters when a later answer cites the acquisition observation: it should preserve what was measured rather than reconstructing unrecorded component timings from arithmetic on independently aggregated numbers.

## Request cohort construction

A cohort is a set of comparable requests, not every row emitted in the observation window. Health probes, cancelled clients and successful checkout requests have different paths and cannot be blended into a business latency average. The proposed review groups by replica generation and checkout route before examining wait time. A missing span is marked missing rather than zero; replacing it with zero would bias the apparent improvement. The cohort manifest should retain exclusions so another reviewer can reproduce the interpretation without treating missing observations as healthy ones.

An observation review should distinguish arrival cohorts from completion cohorts. Requests that arrive near the end of a window may finish outside it, and a completion-only selection can leave their waiting time unrepresented. The synthetic review proposes following each selected arrival until completion, cancellation or the declared observation cutoff. Cutoff requests remain censored observations rather than being recorded as successful zero-duration calls. A separate comparison can use completed work, but its denominator must be explicit. This is especially important when a change improves short requests while a smaller long-running group remains queued. A single average could suggest uniform recovery even though the admission experience differs sharply between those groups. No new measured cohort results are asserted by this proposed review.

Sampling needs a stable relationship to the request population. If tracing retains errors at a higher rate than successes, raw trace proportions do not estimate the application error rate without accounting for that policy. If sampling drops long spans under resource pressure, an apparently healthier window may simply contain less difficult evidence. The report should name the sampling rule, identify changes between compared windows and avoid inventing weights for an undocumented rule. Labels that distinguish checkout routes can help, but high-cardinality merchant identifiers are neither required nor appropriate for this synthetic material. Cohort comparison is an evidential operation: its purpose is to make the retained evidence comparable, not to select a flattering subset or to create production measurements that were never captured.

## Replica multiplication

A per-process pool maximum is not the database's total possible connection count. Two replicas can each reserve leases, and a deployment overlap can briefly retain both old and new replicas. Payments API reliability must compare the aggregate requested concurrency with database limits and resident memory at the selected topology. A value copied from a single-replica rehearsal omits this multiplication. The review records steady-state and overlap topology separately, since a safe steady-state envelope does not automatically permit the extra concurrency during a rolling replacement.

The topology review should treat replica counts as time-varying rather than as one deployment setting read after the incident. A rolling replacement can keep terminating replicas alive while new replicas begin accepting traffic; a draining process may still hold transactions and leases. Multiplying a pool maximum by only the final desired count misses that overlap. The proposed inventory records active, warming and draining generations at each observation boundary. It also distinguishes configured maxima from observed open connections, since a maximum is an upper bound and not proof of actual usage. A planning envelope can reason about the upper bound, whereas an incident explanation needs observations of what the workload actually consumed. Confusing these roles can either hide potential pressure or falsely describe potential as measured.

Other clients share the database concurrency budget even if they do not share this application's pool. Background reconciliation, maintenance and diagnostic clients can occupy server resources while checkout traffic is healthy in isolation. The review should reserve room for known classes of concurrent work and leave unknown consumption explicit instead of assigning it a convenient zero. It must also distinguish a database session limit from CPU, lock or memory constraints that may bind first. None of these considerations determines a replacement numeric maximum in the fixture. They explain why a replica-local restoration needs a workload-specific capacity review and why copying that local number into another service's configuration would skip relevant resource consumers, deployment overlap and the actual limiting dimension.

## Cold and warm paths

Cold-start delay and pool saturation can coexist, but they need different controls. Warm replicas in the recorded slow cohort still waited for leases, so startup alone did not account for the episode. A cold-only test would miss that evidence. Reviewers should keep time-since-start beside acquisition spans and compare warm requests at the same load. They should not discard cold requests to manufacture a good percentile; exclusions belong in the report with their rationale. A warmed workload can still run out of leases when concurrency rises beyond the tested envelope.

Warm-up can alter several components at once: connection creation, compiled query paths, local caches and the number of requests admitted by the readiness gate. An experiment that changes the warm-up routine and the pool maximum together cannot attribute every improvement to one factor. The proposed comparison keeps an unchanged warm-up routine while varying the reviewed pool setting, then separately examines the startup path. If that separation is not feasible, the report names the bundled intervention and avoids a single-cause conclusion. Startup age is retained as context, not used to erase an inconvenient warm-request cohort. The original warm-replica evidence still rules out startup as the only explanation for the recorded waits, without establishing that startup contributed nothing anywhere in the request population.

Pre-opening connections may move cost earlier in time instead of eliminating it. A large burst of replica starts can synchronize authentication and connection setup, creating a short-lived load spike before normal checkout traffic arrives. A synthetic planning review therefore asks whether warm-up is staggered, whether readiness waits for useful initialization and whether cancellation interrupts startup cleanly. It does not report those policies as implemented. A pod that passes a shallow readiness check may still be cold on the business route; conversely, a deliberately delayed readiness gate can keep a cold pod out of the request cohort. These different mechanisms should appear as alternatives with discriminating observations, rather than being collapsed into an unsupported assertion that every slow request was a cold start.

## Response loss and business outcomes

The checkout idempotency investigation is related operational context, not another measurement of pool capacity. A caller may lose a response after a ledger commit, which leaves the business outcome different from the transport outcome. Repeating that request without consulting the merchant-scoped ledger can create a duplicate effect even if connection acquisition has improved. The capacity review therefore keeps timeout counts separate from committed-effect counts. A reduced gateway timeout rate cannot certify idempotency, and an idempotency replay cannot establish memory headroom.

The business-effect review requires a different join than the latency review. A transport request identifier helps pair spans, but a merchant-scoped idempotency key and normalized payload digest identify the intended business operation across retries. Counting HTTP successes alone can miss a committed transaction whose response was lost; counting every retry as a new purchase can overstate effects. The recorded checkout material illustrates this ambiguity, while the capacity notebook does not claim another ledger experiment was executed. A useful handoff states which identity belongs to transport and which belongs to the retained outcome, and keeps missing ledger lookups unresolved. It must not infer that a timeout rolled back a commit just because the caller could not observe the response within its deadline.

Retries can also change the load offered to the pool. A client that repeats an ambiguous write may increase acquisition attempts even if the original business operation completes once. A rate comparison should separate original operations from transport attempts and identify retry delay, maximum attempts and the observation boundary. Otherwise a smaller pool wait could be attributed to capacity when it actually resulted from a calmer retry policy. The converse is possible: a restored pool may admit a retry burst that exposes duplicate-effect weaknesses elsewhere. These are mechanisms to investigate, not fabricated findings. The notebook preserves the independence of the two acceptance gates: reducing acquisition delay does not certify business-effect uniqueness, and a durable idempotency lookup does not prove that the system can sustain the intended concurrency without excessive resident memory.

## Memory headroom qualification

Restoring a pool maximum to 100 recovered this recorded workload; it is not a universal pool recommendation. The healthy observation lasted twenty minutes and did not include peak-load resident-memory measurements. Capacity validation and owner sign-off remain open. A larger maximum can let more work contend for server resources and increase memory per replica. The relevant safety envelope is workload-specific, including replica count, concurrency, query mix and lease lifetime. Advice that omits these limits turns a bounded recovery into an unsupported deployment default.

A capacity envelope should state the dimensions that were exercised rather than only the pool number that changed. Relevant dimensions include concurrent demand, replica topology, query mix, transaction duration, resident memory and the observation duration. Recording the intended envelope before a proposed replay helps prevent the acceptance criteria from drifting after a favorable sample. A measurement missing one dimension can still be useful, but its conclusion must name the omission. In this fixture, the recovered latency window supports incident recovery; it does not fill the missing peak-load memory dimension. There is no approved replacement target and no claim that a general service limit can be computed from the healthy sample. A later summary should keep the open gate adjacent to its recommendation even if it retrieves them separately.

A warning band is a review signal, not automatically an out-of-memory termination or a measured server failure. It needs context about baseline usage, growth during the replay and the configured resource envelope. A steady high working set, a transient allocation burst and unbounded growth would lead to different investigations. The later synthetic warning observation establishes only that the reviewed replay reached that band; it does not establish a memory leak, a crash or a new safe maximum. The distinction prevents an overcorrection in which a model erases a real bounded recovery and replaces it with a fabricated total failure. Accurate advice can acknowledge recovered waits while requiring headroom review before broader adoption, without assuming either that all larger pools are unsafe or that improved latency proves their safety.

## Lease lifetime inspection

Lease duration can rise even when individual command execution is short. Application work performed while holding a connection, transaction scope and delayed disposal can occupy slots that look idle from the database's point of view. The proposed diagnostic compares lease lifetime to execution spans and looks for cancellation paths that fail to release promptly. It must not claim a leak just because one sample is long. A retained trace needs the acquisition, release and cancellation boundaries; an unpaired span remains an uncertainty requiring follow-up rather than a confirmed resource leak.

Transaction scope affects lease occupancy even when a database command is fast. A connection held across application serialization, external calls or a user-facing workflow can remain unavailable to other requests without executing SQL continuously. The proposed trace review pairs lease acquisition and disposal with transaction boundaries and records whether the code awaited unrelated work inside that interval. A long lease may be intentional for consistency, so the first observation should not be labeled a defect without examining the contract. The notebook offers a discriminating question: is the connection held because a transaction must remain open, because disposal was delayed, or because the instrumentation failed to capture release? Those alternatives require different evidence and different corrective proposals.

Cancellation adds a second lifecycle boundary. The caller may abandon its response while the application still owns a connection or waits for the database to acknowledge cancellation. Immediately returning that connection to the reusable pool can be unsafe if its state is uncertain; holding it indefinitely can reduce useful capacity. A reviewed client-library contract determines what reset, disposal or quarantine is needed, not a generic remembered tip. The fixture does not invent library-specific commands or certify such behavior. It asks the future investigator to retain cancellation time, release outcome and uncertainty. That preserves a meaningful distinction between an expected cleanup delay and a confirmed leak, and avoids broadening a timing observation into an unauthorized recovery instruction.

## Queue admission and fairness

Opening more connections is not the only way to reduce waiting. Admission control can bound simultaneous work before it enters the pool, while fairness policies prevent a large slow cohort from starving short requests. Payments API reliability has not selected a new admission policy in this fixture. The comparison asks whether queued work can finish inside caller deadlines and whether retries amplify demand. Dropping requests silently would make successful latency look better while reducing usefulness. Any recommendation must report rejected, timed-out and completed work together.

Admission control should be evaluated against offered demand rather than only completed throughput. A system can show lower latency among admitted requests while rejecting many more callers. The review should therefore retain counts of offered, admitted, queued, rejected and completed attempts together with their deadline classes. A short interactive request and a background reconciliation job may need different treatment, but those classes cannot silently borrow each other's acceptance results. A fairness proposal would identify which queue discipline and isolation boundary it changes; the current fixture selects none. Its purpose is to keep an alternative to pool expansion available for investigation while acknowledging that admission changes have user-visible costs that a successful-request percentile can conceal.

A bounded queue can still retain work whose caller deadline has already expired. Serving that work may occupy a lease without producing a useful response, and repeated retries can create more stale queued attempts. A future diagnostic can compare queue age to remaining deadline and distinguish cancellation before acquisition from cancellation after a transaction begins. It should not assume that removing an expired queued request rolls back an already committed business effect. Load shaping, deadlines and idempotency meet at this boundary but remain separate mechanisms. Any recommendation must describe which boundary it addresses and which outcomes were observed. No admission policy, queue implementation or live execution is supplied by these notes, so a later wiki cannot truthfully present one as an already approved remedy.

## Measurement-window boundaries

Twenty healthy minutes establish an observation window, not all-day durability. A peak shopping period may contain a different request mix or a higher replica count. Windows interrupted by cancellation retain their partial status and should not be glued together as one continuous successful run. A review can compare bounded windows if it names the gap and generation changes. It cannot assume health in the missing interval. Keeping the occurrence time distinct from the time a finding was recorded also prevents a later conclusion from masquerading as knowledge available in the first session.

Time-window comparison needs a consistent treatment of gaps. If observation stops during a worker interruption, the next successful sample begins a new window rather than extending an uninterrupted health claim. The reviewer can report that both bounded windows looked healthy, but should state that the gap is unknown and check whether replica or configuration generation changed during it. The same rule applies to missing telemetry: absence of an error event is not proof that the service was available if the collector was disconnected. The original twenty-minute closure remains a specific observation, not a substitute for every future interval. These distinctions let a future answer be useful without claiming more continuity than the retained sources can support.

Occurrence time and knowledge time serve different questions. A later analyst may record a finding about an earlier replay after correlating its evidence, while an initial session could not have acted on that conclusion yet. A timeline of what happened should use the occurrence boundary; a timeline of decisions should also retain when the relevant finding became available. Mixing them can make the original hypothesis look irrational by supplying it with facts learned later. This notebook preserves the evolving explanation instead of rewriting the first investigation as if it already knew the recovery outcome. The staged fixture release likewise is not a date filter: it intentionally withholds some existing revisions until a later evaluation phase while keeping their original recorded chronology.

## Configuration provenance

A configuration label such as latest is mutable and unsuitable for a precise comparison. The retained review should identify the selected configuration revision and which replicas actually received it. A prepared restoration request is not evidence of execution, and a synthetic recorded approval grants no future authority. When telemetry covers mixed generations, the reviewer can describe that mixture instead of attributing every result to the new setting. Revision-aware interpretation is needed both for latency comparisons and for later corrections to a remembered procedure.

Configuration provenance should identify both requested state and observed state. A deployment request can select an immutable revision while some replicas continue running an earlier configuration. A comparison that attributes the entire traffic window to the requested revision can then conflate generations. The proposed review retains configuration identity per observed replica when that evidence exists and calls the window mixed when it does not. It distinguishes a prepared request, an accepted deployment and a reported application outcome. The synthetic restoration record does not authorize any later deployment, even if its selected setting is remembered accurately. Provenance makes advice inspectable; it does not convert historical approval into standing permission for a tool or an assistant to mutate a service.

A later source correction also needs revision-aware interpretation. Replacing an active document does not create an independent measurement that corroborates its earlier version; it updates what that source currently says while retaining a historical relationship. If an answer uses the older revision's unqualified sentence after a replacement, the evaluator should inspect whether retrieval resolved the wrong active revision or synthesis ignored the caveat. Those are different failure modes and should not be hidden by duplicating both versions into the same active collection. The fixture provides source and revision mappings externally for this purpose. Actual service IDs and index-generated fragment IDs are allocated at runtime and cannot honestly be inferred from the numbered import filename or these authored sections.

## Shared infrastructure comparison

Identity token rotation also uses AKS, but its verification boundary concerns signing-key overlap and verifier caches rather than connection leases. Pod readiness belongs to the infrastructure layer shared by both initiatives. It cannot transfer Identity's rehearsal acceptance milestone into a Payments capacity approval. Conversely, a recovered Payments latency sample says nothing about whether every Identity verifier accepts a newly signed token. Shared technology is useful navigation context, while project outcomes still require project-specific evidence and exclusions.

Infrastructure dependencies can explain where to look without deciding what was completed. A readiness endpoint, a deployment generation and a shared cluster schedule may be relevant to both Payments API reliability and Identity token rotation. Their relevance does not make a pool-acquisition finding an authentication-acceptance finding. A comparison should name the shared dependency, then state each application's business boundary and independent unknowns. The same principle applies to a shared incident channel or a common reviewer: social proximity does not transfer status. In this fixture the reader can use the AKS mention to navigate across related initiatives while still retaining separate recovery, capacity, overlap and rollout statements grounded in the appropriate source evidence.

A dependency fault can also affect those applications differently. A restarted replica might lose a local cache in one application and rebuild a connection pool in another, producing different transient symptoms under the same infrastructure event. Similar timing is reason to investigate a common trigger, not proof of an identical mechanism. The proposed review would compare application-specific spans or acceptance cases on the same generation rather than promoting a shared platform label into a root cause. No such cross-application fault experiment was executed here. The authored comparison deliberately preserves separate hypotheses so a future synthesis can discuss common context without merging field ownership or announcing that one team's completed local milestone closed another team's unresolved gate.

## Contrasting memory-warning observation

A later synthetic replay at 100 concurrent requests reached the memory warning band even though acquisition waits improved. This contrasts with the earlier healthy latency window rather than invalidating the recorded incident recovery. It narrows what can be recommended: memory and aggregate concurrency must be reviewed before adopting the same maximum elsewhere. The fixture does not establish a replacement numeric target. A reviewer should retain both the successful bounded recovery and the warning evidence, with capacity approval still unresolved rather than rewriting history as either total failure or universal success.

The contrasting warning is valuable because it challenges the extrapolation, not because it erases the earlier measurement. Improved acquisition waits and elevated resident memory can both be true in one replay. The former describes responsiveness at the pool boundary, while the latter concerns a resource envelope. A useful evidence comparison keeps both outcomes with their load and observation context. It does not invent a crash, a production incident or a replacement safe value from the warning alone. An evaluator should look for advice that remains operationally bounded: recognize the recovered incident, explain why the new finding narrows applicability and leave the capacity decision unresolved until the intended workload envelope and responsible review supply the missing evidence.

The next discriminating proposal should separate memory consumed by pooled resources from memory associated with admitted application work. Comparing a controlled request mix, replica topology and lease lifetime can help determine which mechanism changes with load. A future measurement might use several candidate settings, but this fixture has not run that comparison and establishes no winning configuration. A summary that supplies a new number would therefore fabricate an outcome rather than distill evidence. The late note uses resident-memory wording and explicit earlier-record references to exercise discovery beyond existing citations. This makes the update case about finding and applying a relevant qualification, while the source history still records the successful bounded recovery and the distinction between a proposed measurement and an executed operational change.
